agents.answer: Deeper look: in last week's logs 63 of 70 approvals were a plain 'yes' or '好的', which is what the fast path speeds up (about 1.2 s each). Removing it means the model sees every reply; the risk is a slow answer on an urgent approval. A middle way: keep a tiny allow list of exact one-word replies ('yes', '好') and send anything longer to the model, which would have caught the '好的继续，不过先跑测试' case.

key_points: About 1,500 characters of hand-written regular expressions and word lists match short replies such as 好的, 继续, yes or wait.
Those matches are turned straight into an approve key or a cancel without asking the model.
A whole sentence is matched on its first words, so a condition after it (a 'but ...') is lost; this bypasses the rule that the model decides.
There are three word lists for the same meanings in three files and they disagree (for example 行 approves in one file but not in another).
Example: '好的继续，不过先跑测试' was approved in 40 ms and the 'run the tests first' part never reached the model.
The safety rule that refuses dangerous keys should stay in code.
Recommendation: delete the word lists (about 300 lines) and send every reply to the model, at a cost of about 1.2 seconds more latency on a plain yes.

agents.answer: Ran the test 200 times with the race detector: 17 failures, every one with the price cache empty when the request arrived. With a wait on Ready() added locally: 0 failures in 200 runs. The race exists since the 'parallel cache warm-up' change three weeks ago, which moved the warm-up into a background goroutine.

key_points: The checkout totals test fails about 1 run in 12 (7 of 84 runs this week).
Cause: the test sends its request before the price cache has finished warming up (a race).
With an empty cache the handler uses list prices, so the total misses the 15% member discount (100 instead of 85).
It blocked two deploys last week, each needing a manual re-run of about 25 minutes.
It is a test problem, not a production bug: production warms the cache before taking traffic.
Recommended fix: wait for the cache's ready signal in the test setup (about 3 lines); the alternative is a fake cache.
Nothing has been changed yet.

agents.answer: The ledger was added in July with a cap of 5 to keep the brain's prompt short; each note costs about 40 tokens, so even 10 notes would add only about 400 tokens. The delete tool would be a 'forget' tool the brain can call with the note's words; it would refuse to delete a note the CEO marked as a rule unless asked twice.

key_points: The notes ledger keeps at most 5 notes; a 6th note silently pushes the oldest one out.
All 5 slots are used and 2 notes are stale (a release date that has passed, a worker that no longer exists).
The next note will push out 'always ask before pushing to main', the oldest and most important note.
A delete tool would let the CEO remove stale notes by voice; it is about 60 lines plus tests.
It is useful but not urgent: nothing is lost until a 6th note is added.
The alternative is raising the cap to 10, which only delays the problem and keeps stale notes.

agents.answer: Checked the provider's docs: the limit is 100 calls per minute per API key, and the bulk endpoint counts as one call however many invoices it carries (up to 500). The job's last success sent 87 invoices on 2026-10-04. Customers on annual plans are billed on the 1st, so the 4,200 spike repeats every month.

key_points: The nightly invoice job sends one payment-provider API call per invoice.
Last night had 4,200 invoices but the provider allows 100 calls per minute, so the calls were rejected as too many requests.
The job has no retry, so 4,100 invoices were not sent; customers get them a day late unless it is re-run before 9:00.
It worked before because there were fewer than 100 invoices a night; the new annual plans pushed it to 4,200 on the 1st.
Proper fix: the bulk endpoint takes 500 invoices per call (9 calls), about 40 lines.
Quick fix: retry with a one-minute wait (about 42 minutes); re-running is safe because duplicate invoice ids are ignored.
